description: We are Space Wanderers, a dynamic team excited to participate in NASA Space Apps 2026! Our team brings together diverse talents in programming, data analysis, and problem-solving. We're passionate about tackling complex challenges and pushing the boundaries of innovation. We can explore new frontiers and solve real-world problems. Let's make this mission a success!
summary:
In Colombia, victims of the armed conflict returning to their land under Law 1448 of 2011 face uncertainty about what to grow and how to generate sustainable income. PaisAgro supports small and medium-sized producers in Western Antioquia through satellite data, artificial intelligence, and local knowledge.

The platform integrates NASA POWER, GPM/IMERG, SENTINEL, and local socioeconomic data into a harmonized territorial model, accessible through a REST API. Its transparent agronomic engine converts scientific literature into actionable recommendations, displaying confidence levels, supporting evidence, and missing data. Agronomists can validate and adjust rules without programming.

AgroAstro, an AI-powered advisor and research agent, evaluates crop rotation plans, explains recommendations, and searches external sources—including government websites, institutional programs, technical documents, scientific publications, and PDFs—to enrich its answers with relevant information.

The offline-ready mobile app features a 3D globe with satellite layers, community radio, educational games, voice narration, and market prices, bringing accessible agricultural intelligence to rural communities and supporting sustainable livelihoods and productive land restitution.
details:
Introduction

Can NASA data help a farmer put farming strategies into practice without losing sight of their socioeconomic and geopolitical context?

For decades, Colombia’s countryside has been marked by armed conflict, land dispossession and forced displacement. Along the way, campesino identity and the community knowledge that sustained local production chains were pushed aside. Under Law 1448 of 2011 (the Victims and Land Restitution Law), many victims of the armed conflict have been able to return to their land. But they come back to an uncertain picture: they do not know the current productive conditions of their plots, how the land should be used, or what could generate income. Getting the land back is only the first step. The real challenge is turning recovered plots into sustainable agricultural systems.

Context

This is the reality of many small and medium-sized producers in Western Antioquia, the region we chose as our case study. The region is known for its agricultural production, its crop exports and a strong tradition of community knowledge exchange. It is also one of the subregions of Antioquia where maize, beans and squash, the three crops of the traditional Three Sisters system, are all documented, and in 2023 it recorded the largest squash production among the subregions we compared (1,512 tonnes). Yet the territory was historically built around cash crops such as coffee, panela sugarcane, plantain and avocado, and maize and beans have shrunk into crops for household consumption. Families who recover their land often do not know what to plant or how to care for their soil. Technical assistance exists, but it is fragmented and rarely reaches every vereda. Limited connectivity, few devices and reading difficulties keep technical information out of reach.

At the same time, information about the land has never been more abundant. NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and the European Sentinel-2 satellites measure precipitation, temperature, moisture and vegetation across the entire territory. But this data is scattered across independent agencies and published in formats and resolutions that do not match, so it rarely reaches the people who work the land. Even when it does, it is not enough on its own: an agricultural decision cannot be made with agroclimatic data alone. A recommendation that ignores a family’s history, its security situation, its markets and its traditional knowledge will not be adopted, however accurate it is.

That is why we created PaisAgro. PaisAgro combines local information, data from space agencies and the socioeconomic context of the territory to generate crop rotation and soil care recommendations for small and medium-sized producers in Western Antioquia who are victims of the armed conflict. It works through a web platform with farmer and technician profiles, voice interaction, educational games, local market prices and radio programs aired by community stations. That way, the knowledge reaches the families who need it most, including those without a device or an internet connection. Our goal is to help restituted land become an opportunity for a dignified life, while strengthening campesino identity and Colombia’s food sovereignty.

Below is the territorial agroclimatic intelligence architecture that was designed to close the following gaps identified between ideation and creation:

·         An agricultural decision cannot be made with agroclimatic data alone:  We gave priority to the idea that one pillar of the project is the ability to communicate with, and engage with, the farmers' social, ecological, economic and geopolitical context. It makes no sense to propose crop rotations, strategies or proposals without knowing the local context beyond the data.

 

·         Source heterogeneity: We realized that the data is scattered across independent missions and agencies, and that there is no unified, source-agnostic model per study variable that allows a territory to be analyzed directly in terms of hydrological variables.

 

·         Data type heterogeneity: Missions that measure the same variable differ in their first-level data in terms of type, spatial location, time, resolution, among others. This is natural, since different missions do not share the same instruments, overpasses, etc.

 

·         Data structure heterogeneity: We identified structured information sources, including cases where a source from a space or local agency does not provide API services to query the information in JSON or other formats. We also identified unstructured or plain-format information sources such as laws and government documentation in PDF, web news, the farmers' own experience, among others.

 

·         Data volume:  To recommend and analyze patterns, a considerable temporal, spatial and variable range must be taken into account, which is not feasible in real time for a fast, easily accessible web application that communicates directly with NASA services while skipping data quality and data engineering processes.

 

Based on these premises, the following decisions were made and the solution was designed.

Technical requirements of the architecture:

·          With this in mind, we needed to build an easily accessible capability that could serve as the foundation for a natural-language recommendation engine or a web application, directly linking an area of interest with a study variable, independently of the sources, for agricultural projects, by querying a data lake.

 

·         Offline pipelines were built to carry out extraction, data quality and canonicalization, grouping by precipitation, vegetation, soil information and wind speed characteristics 

 

·         The solution was built with a modular design communicating via REST services, which allows separating the integration and extraction layers for the source data, the service and data storage layer for online consumption from a data lake, and the recommendations layer. The service and storage layer was managed by the agronomic intelligence engine, which in turn queried the territorial canonical model according to the spatio-temporal information needs.

 

·         Online consumption via API was separated from offline processing, which makes analysis-ready data available in the data lake for cross-referencing with other sources. For integrations that were not possible due to connectivity limitations, the data was downloaded manually and imported locally to produce the first data seed.

·         Real geometry data was used for territorial aggregation by area of interest, using GeoPackages obtained from Mapas Colombia, from which we built a master grid that we called “Grid Master”.

 

·         A REST API service was made available that receives requests for recommendations and agroclimatic analysis of a territory and returns them based on the canonical model. This API enabled integration with the web platform, with AI agents specialized in tasks such as automatically creating radio broadcast programs based on the recommendation engine, and with the generation of administrative or government reports by custom areas of interest or by regional segmentation.

Documentación API Canonical: https://api-canonica-production.up.railway.app/docs

An architecture was designed and implemented to reduce the friction of turning raw data into information, identifying changes, among others. Each module was built in Python, where AI was used as a means and not as an end. Understanding that programming is a means to deliver solutions and improve quality of life, we prioritized the creative process and an abstract, agnostic design focused on the need to relate agroclimatic variables, territory and its context. An offline pipeline was run to extract data from different sources for a territory of interest, through web services when available or through manual downloads from web providers, which are detailed in this project's references. Next, each source went through a validation stage in which cleaning, data quality and data validation were performed by comparing against real values, using pipelines with AI agents. Afterwards, the sources were homogenized in terms of physical measurement, temporal reference and spatial reference, and the original sources were kept for reference to preserve traceability to the origin. Once the data had been homogenized, the following was ensured:

·         A common unit and statistic per variable

·         Unified temporal resolution

·         Cell-based spatial reference linking coordinates and geometries

·         Clean data

·         Geospatial and temporal coverage

 

Next, the sources were unified into the common canonical model, which had the following structure:

#

Field

Type

Description and role within the canonical model

1

grid_id

String

Cell identifier. Links each observation to a cell of the master grid (grid_master.gpkg). Allows different variables and sources to be integrated over the same spatial unit.

2

variable

String

Canonical variable. Identifies the measured phenomenon, regardless of the source. Example: precipitation_amount.

3

unit

String

Unit of measurement. Sets the normalized unit used to compare observations. Example: mm.

4

statistic

String

Statistical operation. Indicates how the value is represented over the observed period. Example: sum corresponds to accumulated precipitation.

5

time_start

Datetime

Period start. Defines when the observation starts to apply. Enables temporal queries and comparisons.

6

time_end

Datetime

Period end. Sets the end boundary of the interval, used as an exclusive endpoint in this dataset.

7

source

String

Information source. Identifies the entity, mission or system that provides the measurement. Example: NASA POWER, GPM_IMERG.

8

product

String

Source product. Specifies the dataset used within a source. Example: PRECTOTCORR or GPM_3IMERGHHL.

9

version

String / Null

Product version. Makes it possible to identify dataset revisions and ensure traceability.

10

processing_run

String / Null

Processing mode. Identifies the processing run or category of the product, such as LATE in GPM.

11

value

Float

Observation value. Contains the numeric magnitude of the variable for a given cell and period. It is the main data point consumed by the agroclimatic engine.

12

spatial_coverage

Float

Spatial coverage. Represents the proportion of the target cell covered by source data. A value of 1.0 indicates virtually complete coverage according to the geometry used.

13

temporal_coverage

Float/ Null

Temporal coverage. Indicates what proportion of the expected period has valid observations. A value of 1.0 represents full coverage; null means it was not reported

 

 

14

quality_flag

String

Quality flag. Classifies the validity status of the observation. Example: valid. Allows records to be filtered before analysis.

15

spatial_method

String

Spatial harmonization method. Indicates how the data was transferred from its original representation to the master grid. Example: area_weighted_mean.

16

contributing_cells

Integer

Contributing source cells. Counts how many source cells took part in calculating the value assigned to a target cell.

17

spatial_id

String

Normalized spatial identifier. Identifies the spatial support unit of the observation. In this dataset it matches grid_id.

18

spatial_support

String

Spatial support type. Describes the geographic unit on which the value is interpreted. Example: master_grid_cell, which corresponds to a cell of the master grid.

19

latitude

Float

Reference latitude. Geographic coordinate associated with the cell, useful for spatial queries, visualization and location.

20

longitude

Float

Reference longitude. Complements the latitude to spatially locate the observation.

21

input_file

String

Source file. Records the processed file from which the canonical data point originated. Facilitates audits, reproducibility of results and debugging.

22

geometry_status

String

Geometric validation status. Describes whether the geometry used in spatial harmonization is verified or was built through approximations. Helps assess spatial reliability.

 

During development, several tkinter viewers were implemented and later migrated to the web app to explore the data we analyzed interactively and visually.

In addition, to make it easier to work with geojson, parquet and other files, tools were developed to speed up the research and development process, such as:

 

·         Parquet-to-JSON converter

This canonical model was designed so that it can be integrated with a data lake for the real-time service and consumption layer, and deliver the recommendations in a JSON structure to an AI agent. The agent was given context to receive the JSON with the recommendations provided by the agro-economic engine, based on the measurements provided by the canonical variable model, and to additionally query web data sources.

Agronomic engine

The engine is a transparent rule system, not a black box. Its knowledge lives in an agronomic notebook of biological claims drawn from technical literature. The claims cover:

Plant nutrition: the role of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and how each deficiency shows on the leaves.

Soil chemistry: acidity, aluminium toxicity and liming.

Crop physiology: C4 crops, thermal time and light capture.

Water and climate: crop water demand by growth stage, and root damage from waterlogging.

Pests: the fall armyworm and the stem borer Diatraea.

Diseases: bean anthracnose, Sigatoka and the disease triangle.

Crop associations: the Three Sisters and nitrogen fixation by legumes.

Management: rotation, mulching and cover crops.

Satellite monitoring: NDVI, canopy temperature and SMAP soil moisture.

Each claim also has a role in the engine:

Some become rules the engine can test with today’s data.

Some become rules that wait for a variable not yet available.

Some become low-cost management practices.

Some stay as explanatory knowledge that backs the “Why” card.

For example, the claim that “below pH 5.5, aluminium becomes soluble, damages roots and locks up phosphorus” becomes the rule soil_ph < 5.5. The claims on nitrogen depletion and the stem borer that sugarcane and maize share become a rule that blocks planting them together or one after the other. Each rule records:

its condition: a variable, an operator and a threshold;

the crops and growth stages it applies to;

its severity and its starting confidence (low or moderate; no rule starts at high);

the claims it comes from.

For each plot, every rule ends in one of three states: it fires, it stays silent, or it reports “cannot decide” when a value is missing or its range straddles the threshold. Then 86 interactions let the rules talk to each other. 52 modifiers act as weights: 37 raise a finding’s confidence by one level when another signal supports it, 5 lower it by one level when another signal contradicts it, and 10 have weight 0 so that a coincidence cannot inflate confidence. 29 syntheses merge signals into one diagnosis, and 5 precedence rules let the specific alert lead. The certainty shown to the farmer is the weakest of three factors: the rule’s confidence, where its threshold came from, and the quality of the data behind it.

Because all of this lives in the notebook rather than the code, an agronomist can apply their own judgement without programming. They can:

move a threshold, for example maize heat stress at flowering from 35 °C to 33 °C for a local variety;

restrict a rule to certain crops or stages;

change a rule’s severity or starting confidence;

re-weight a modifier anywhere from −2 to +2, or set it to 0 to block an inference the evidence does not support.

When the engine loads the notebook, it audits every edit and keeps each rule tied to its original claim. The API picks up the changes on its next restart. From the app, the agronomist also downloads a review sheet and marks each rule as validated, to adjust or rejected. Today 150 rules have a documentary review of their sources, but none has been validated in the field, so certainty is capped at “medium”. Rejected rules stop running, and only rules a technician validates can reach “high”. This way the engine improves with local expertise instead of replacing it.

AI-powered assistant agent for agricultural decision-making

 The AI agent was created on the OpenAI platform and was given the prompt located in the same folder as this document. The agent was conditioned with various query rules, specific sources to consider per territory, behavioral restrictions, among others, all of which are described in detail in the agent's base prompt.

 

 

PaisAgro App

Field Shift puts NASA satellite data in a farmer's pocket. It works with one hand, uses plain language and keeps the evidence in view.

Experience

Live 3D globe: smooth flights over a dark space view and 9 NASA data layers: vegetation greenness (NDVI), soil moisture, rainfall, daytime and nighttime surface temperature, evapotranspiration, groundwater, terrain and risk zones across Colombia.

NASA missions: SMAP, GPM/IMERG, MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat-HLS, ECOSTRESS, GRACE-FO, SRTM and NASA POWER.

Instant location: first by IP, then by GPS. The globe flies straight to your area.

Time machine: see how your land looked months ago.

Region panel: tap the map to see what the sensors say about that area.

Artificial intelligence

Real-time crop rotation plan: draw your farm and the plan starts on its own. Watch each step as it happens: your area's data → agronomic engine → review by AgroAstro, our AI advisor.

An assistant that moves the map: ask a question and it answers, then flies the globe, turns on layers and opens panels.

Farm radio: every place has its own station. The daily show is built from real data and moves the globe sentence by sentence.

Inclusion

Learn by playing: pick a character, play 7 challenges, earn points and take one-minute lessons in AgroAcademy.

Built for everyone: simple mode, sun mode (high contrast), voice narrator, Spanish and English, keyboard navigation and a "what is this?" for every technical term.

Honesty: every recommendation shows its confidence, the data it's missing and its risks. The tool supports farmers' judgment; it doesn't replace it.

Community: listed farms with WhatsApp contact, community event reports and market prices.

Engineering

Mobile first and offline-ready: designed for 360 px screens. It installs as an app (PWA) and keeps your latest analysis for when you're offline.

Lightweight: under 150 KB on first load, with the globe designed to run at 60 fps on a mid-range Android phone.

Reliable: strict TypeScript, every API response validated and 20 end-to-end test suites on a Pixel 7.
